entities.name: Erasmus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam (1466–1536) was a Dutch Renaissance humanist, Catholic priest, and theologian who was the most influential scholar of the Northern Renaissance. His satirical masterpiece 'In Praise of Folly' (1509) mocked the corruption of the Catholic Church, and his Greek New Testament (1516) provided the textual basis for Protestant Bible translations.

Erasmus corresponded with virtually every major intellectual in Europe — his network of over 3,000 surviving letters constitutes the first pan-European 'Republic of Letters.' He advocated reform within the Catholic Church through education and moral persuasion rather than schism, earning him criticism from both Catholics and Protestants.

When Martin Luther's Reformation erupted in 1517, Erasmus initially sympathized but ultimately refused to join, famously declaring: 'I laid a hen's egg; Luther hatched a bird of quite a different kind.' His commitment to moderation in an age of extremism made him both admired and distrusted by all sides.
